articles.content:
The Australian Film Festival of India (AFFI) is back after a COVID-era hiatus, staging screenings across Indian cities through Dec. 22 alongside a new industry strand aimed at pulling Indian producers and investors toward Australia as the India-Australia Audio Visual Co-Production Treaty takes effect.

AFFI made its debut in Mumbai in 2011, backed by Hugh Jackman, and later editions drew support from Baz Luhrmann and Phillip Noyce. Festival director Peter Castaldi now oversees the relaunch. The centerpiece of the industry push is the Screen Australia-backed Australian Cinema Bootcamp, which will run full-day sessions in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Trivandrum, with more cities to be added. The sessions are pitched at Indian producers and directors as well as investors, distributors, students and VFX and post houses. Topics include co-producing under the new treaty, putting money into Australian films and India-focused Australian projects, government and state incentives such as the Producer Offset, cross-border distribution, and access to Australian VFX, post-production, locations and specialist crews.

Money is a big part of the pitch. Australia's Producer Offset refunds 40% of qualifying local spend on eligible feature films, and states offer their own grants and attraction funds. Together, the incentives lower how much capital investors put at risk.

"This is an exciting time to strengthen screen industry ties between Australia and India," said Grainne Brunsdon, Screen Australia's chief operating officer. "Having had a delegation of producers at WAVES Film Bazaar , Screen Australia is proud to support this series of Australian Cinema Bootcamp, which provides filmmakers from Australia and India with more opportunities to connect, collaborate and create new pathways for stories that celebrate the richness and diversity of our shared cultural connections." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Disney Studios, Ausfilm, the City of Perth and the University of NSW are among the institutions supporting the festival itself. Ausfilm CEO Kate Marks said the organization welcomed moves to draw the two industries closer and, as Australia's film commission, was on hand to help Indian filmmakers make use of the country's production and post-production capabilities. "Initiatives like Screen Australia's delegation to Goa and the Australian Film Festival of India are a great way to build connections and open the door to more collaboration," she said.

On the screening side, the lineup features "First Light," Australia's official submission for the international feature Oscar; "Brand Bollywood Downunder," from AFFI founding creative director Anupam Sharma, which features well-known names from the Indian film business; and "UnIndian," starring Brett Lee. Indian-origin Australians including producer Chetan Oberoi and Yogi Devgan will also be showcased.

"Indian cinema has conquered the world on its own terms. Australia offers Indian storytellers something rare: a bigger canvas, world-class crews and post-production, government support which reduces financial risks in the film, and a system that delivers on time and on budget," said Sharma. "We want to see Indian money, Indian stories and Australian know-how in the same film, on screens around the world."

Partners in several Indian cities have signed on. The International Film Festival of Kerala will present a handpicked slate of Australian titles and a panel, while Shanmugam and AVM Studios will host the Chennai leg.

"The showcase brings the best of new Australian cinema to Indian audiences," said Castaldi, who added that AFFI is also putting a spotlight on the expanding pool of Australian screen talent with Indian roots.

Lisa Sthalekar , the India-born cricketer who was adopted out of a Pune orphanage and later became one of Australia's leading international players, is the subject of a feature film in development at "Wedding Season" star Pallavi Sharda 's Bodhini Studios.

The company has secured the rights to the life story of Sthalekar, now a cricket commentator, and Sharda describes it as the flagship feature on the studio's slate. "We've been really working hard to bring the right voices," Sharda tells Variety . "What differentiates the way we're working as a diaspora group of artists is making sure that our voices are in the room from inception. And it's not something that happens as an afterthought." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Sharda hasn't been officially cast as Sthalekar, though she says the cricketer would like her to play the role. "And the other producers on board, who I can't reveal right now, probably would," she adds.

The film brings together cricket and storytelling, two of the most lasting ties between Australia and India, and centers on a female athlete's story.

Sharda, a Screen Australia board member, is in Goa with the agency's delegation to the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) and the WAVES Film Bazaar . The group hopes to forge alliances through the Australia–India Audiovisual Co-production Agreement, a 2023 pact that lets filmmakers in the two countries work together and draw on qualifying public funding and incentives.

"As a board member of Screen Australia, I have a huge interest in how we tell our stories and how we shape Australian stories for the world," Sharda says. "So for me, the practical steps really come under my guise as a practitioner more than my board role." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Sharda launched Bodhini in 2024, naming it after the feminine of the Bodhi tree. "The idea is to tell stories consciously and to deep dive into the communities that enabled me to be an artist, which was the Indian community of Australia," she says. The company has already run several writers' rooms.

Also on the slate is the feature documentary "Fear and Loathing in Kathmandu," which Sharda is producing with Emmy-nominated Australian filmmaker Gil Marsden ("The Gymkhana Files," "Revealed – Death Cap Murders"). The film is directed by Sparsh Ahuja, a National Geographic Explorer whose VR docu-drama "Child of Empire" premiered at Sundance in 2022. It charts Nepal's journey from 1960s hippie haven, when cannabis was legal, through a U.S.-backed drug crackdown and decades of upheaval, and links it to today's U.S. cannabis boom. Bodhini is also developing a comedy series about the Australian-Indian diaspora in Melbourne. Its title is under wraps while the project sits with a commissioner.

A Perth native who grew up in Melbourne, Sharda learned Hindi and Bharatanatyam in Australia before relocating to Mumbai, where she became a trailblazing Indian-Australian lead in mainstream Bollywood films. Her credits include "Besharam," opposite Ranbir Kapoor, Hollywood's "Tom & Jerry" and Netflix's "Wedding Season," which she led. She also picked up a Logie nomination for her turn opposite Sam Neill in Australian drama "The Twelve."

Sharda credits "Wedding Season" producer Swati Shetty with backing her as she builds her own slate. "The reason my career has been an oscillation between two nations is because of my belief in representation," Sharda says. "I was just at home in Melbourne and we were celebrating Navratri. And I met a lot of aunties after a long time that were with me. And one aunty in particular started crying. She says, 'You were the first, first of our children to be in the newspapers.'"

Shetty, she says, understands that, having made "Wedding Season" and seen its impact on South Asian storytelling. "Now we need to build on that, basically, as diaspora filmmakers," Sharda says.

In front of the camera, Sharda recently wrapped "Stay," Indian filmmaker Rohena Gera's French-language film, which shot in Pune and around Paris. The project, produced by Alice Bloch, is now in post-production and is eyeing a 2027 release. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"As a French-speaking actress, I never thought that I would get the chance to use that skill," Sharda says. "It's a dream for any actor to be able to lead a film where you have to have that one-on-one lock-in time with your director, and it really is the medium of storytelling and filmmaking in its purest form."

On a possible return to mainstream Bollywood, Sharda says: "I have really started to miss it because I'm so Indian. Speaking in Hindi, speaking in kind of the lilts of my Indian self is something I miss."

With a mother from Uttar Pradesh and a father from Punjab, Sharda says the Hindi she speaks is distinctly local, and the inner world that language opens up is something she can only reach in India.

"That part of me is feeling a little bit bereft," she says. "So I would love to."

articles.title: Chris Evans’ Return in Avengers: Doomsday Has Already Spoiled Steve Rogers’ Perfect Arc
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel Avengers: Endgame felt like an event for many reasons. It was the culmination of the Infinity Saga, finally pitting Earth’s Mightiest Heroes against Thanos for one last showdown. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Avengers: Endgame felt like an event for many reasons. It was the culmination of the Infinity Saga , finally pitting Earth’s Mightiest Heroes against Thanos for one last showdown. Aside from its main villain, the plot of the film was shrouded in mystery, with fans left unaware that it all hinged on a journey through the MCU via a “time heist” to retrieve the Infinity Stones and undo the devastating ending of Avengers: Infinity War . It also seemed to be the final Marvel film for both Robert Downey Jr. and Chris Evans , who had anchored the MCU for roughly a decade as the co-leaders of the Avengers franchise. Now both Downey and Evans are back for Avengers: Doomsday , which inevitably raises a ton of questions.

Of course, Downey’s and Evans’ returns couldn’t be more different. After his Tony Stark sacrificed himself to save the universe, Downey is back in the MCU fold this time as Victor von Doom, the titular villain of Avengers: Doomsday . This has left fans puzzling over how, if at all, the MCU’s Doctor Doom will connect to Tony Stark, a question made more confusing by what Marvel has said about the character. Meanwhile, Evans is seemingly back as the same Steve Rogers fans know and love — with magic, time travel, and the multiverse in the mix, who can be sure? — but no matter what Avengers: Doomsday does, the character’s arc has already been spoiled.

In one of their first interactions, Tony Stark and Steve Rogers call each other out. Stark claims that Rogers is only special because of the Super Soldier Serum, while Rogers accuses him of never being willing to lay his own life on the line to save others. But throughout their time on the Avengers together, the two heroes prove each other wrong . Tony is actually the one who makes the sacrifice play, using the Infinity Stones to defeat Thanos and his army at the expense of his own life. And not only is Steve worthy of lifting Mjolnir, but he takes the opportunity to lay down his shield and pursue a life with his beloved Peggy Carter. Here is the original ending of Avengers: Endgame :

Despite the early MCU very much figuring out what it wants to be in real time, the Infinity Saga managed to give its two lead heroes the perfect farewell. After seven films — not including his several uncredited cameos — as Steve Rogers, Evans walked away from Marvel with a sense of completion and satisfaction. By the end of 2019’s Avengers: Endgame , Steve finally gets that dance he promised Peggy in 2011’s Captain America: The First Avenger . And in that moment, the Infinity Saga ends not with an epic battle sequence and not a gotcha stinger teasing what comes next. Instead, it ends on an intimate moment between two characters who have overcome impossible odds for the chance to be together.

Then Avengers Endgame: Encore happened. Among the only new additions to the rerelease is an altered ending that interrupts Steve and Peggy’s hard-earned dance with a knock at the door. It’s Loki, seemingly there to warn them of Doctor Doom’s imminent plans. Cue the events of Avengers: Doomsday . While it might be there to retcon a direct connection between the fourth and fifth Avengers films, this change undercuts everything that has happened in the MCU since, including the pitch-perfect conclusion of Steve’s arc. In a flash, that cathartic ending of Avengers: Endgame is compromised to satisfy the storytelling needs of the larger shared universe. Still, it remains to be seen where Avengers: Doomsday goes from here.

Fans only get a tease of what Steve Rogers — likely officially adopting the Nomad moniker this time — is up to in the fight against Doctor Doom. So it’s anyone’s guess how this all plays out. Likely, if Doom is tied to Stark somehow, Steve is there to emotionally react to his departed friend’s face on this new threat. But it’s very possible that things aren’t exactly as they seem. Marvel has a long history of purposefully misleading fans to preserve the theatrical experience. Will Steve immediately walk away from Peggy to join the fight? Is this even the Steve we know? Or are there some multiversal shenanigans afoot? But for now, the MCU has tarnished Steve and Peggy’s happy ending. Here’s hoping he gets right back to dancing as soon as this latest adventure is over.

Did Marvel ruin the ending of Avengers: Endgame ? If so, can the MCU still recover Steve and Peggy’s happy ending? Let us know in the comments below!

Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters on December 18, 2026.

The Unlabelled Alliance comprises Ex-UTA and Fremantle branded chief Sam Glynne , 7Wonder founder and TV producer Liza Abbott , Somethin' Else director and audio indistry veteran Steve Ackerman , Gleam Futures founder and creator economy talent manager Dom Smales and Little Dot Studios co-founder Selma Turajlic .

Each member of the Unlabelled Alliance will continue to run their own businesses and ventures, and provide tailored advice and support to clients – meaning they can form different combinations and find solutions based on the company.

The coalition is targeting broadcasters, studios, distributors, publishers, music companies, talent agencies, production companies and brands, and is pitching its offer as "experience-based solutions without the burden of fixed overheads." As such they're presenting the advisory as a "deliberately lean, plug-in model" that engages only as long as a problem requires.

Their rationale for the alliance is that the industry is not simply changing, but "fracturing and rebuilding itself in a completely different shape." They note that broadcaster commission budgets are shrinking in many cases, while the creator economy is growing and formats often shift across mediums and platforms. The plan for the business has been in the works for some time, with a website now up and running, and we understand several deals are set to conclude. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“We came together as a group, first as friends and then with a shared vision of using our experience to future-proof the industry that we’ve grown up in," the Unlabelled Alliance co-founders said in a statement.

"We built our careers in traditional media and went on to revolutionise it from the inside out: building and scaling businesses, pioneering digital-first content, creating new models for talent and re-imagining legacy IP potential. We know the pain points because we've been there. Our aim is your innovation and growth."

They added they would be a "hands-on and results-driven advisory team of seasoned specialists, helping C-suites, boards, founders and investors work out what is stopping them scaling and delivering real, smart and swift solutions."

Abbott will provide IP, studios and transformational and operational infrastructure advice. She was most recently the Chief Content Officer at The Earthshot Prize, Prince William's environmental initiative. Prior to that, she was COO of Unscripted at Fremantle, overseeing Thames, Talkback, Boundless and Shotglass. She was co-founder of 7Wonder, the UK production joint venture of Maverick Television and Australia’s Seven Network that's now part of Banijay. Abbott has also held senior roles at Maverick, ITV Studios, IMG and the BBC.

Ackerman plans to offer audio, podcasting and content strategy advice. He is known as one of radio giant and multimedia production pioneer Somethin' Else's early directors, and led the company up to its sale to Sony Music Entertainment, at which point he became EVP and Head of Global Podcasts for the Sony. He is now a non-exec director of The Podcast Show and subscription platform SupaPas.

Glynne is the branded entertainment and IP strategy expert. She founded and was head of UTA's EMEA Entertainment and Culture Marketing business, and worked as Global SVP of Branded Entertainment at Fremantle, working across 30 territories. Prior to that, she ran Renault TV and set up and ran The Audio Channel for All3Media and BBH. She's also a Cannes Lions judge.

Smales, considered by many the architect of the creator economy and influencer world in Europe, will focus on talent and the creator economy solutions. He's known for leading Gleam Futures, the early digital-first talent management business he founded in 2010. In 2021, he exited for Dentsu and now runs WinnieWood, a creator economy group that spans talent management, entertainment IP, commerce, tech and investments, and is a co-founder of creator-led entertainment producer GloMotion Studios.

Turajlic will handle digital transformation and entrepreneurship. She is known as co-founder of Little Dot Studios alongside the late Andy Taylor. The business, which now has well over 500 staff, has been singled out as a key pillar in growth for Banijay, which added Little Dot to its ranks through its acquisition of All3 this year. Turajlic also had senior roles at All3, Sony Pictures Television an Celador International, and is now a venture builder and angel investor with Alma Angels.

articles.content:
An audiovisual co-production treaty between India and Chile has reached the last stage of negotiation, according to Jorge Loyola Castro, Chile's trade commissioner to India, who spoke to Variety at the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

The talks trace back to then-President Gabriel Boric's state visit to India in April 2025, the first by a Chilean president since Michelle Bachelet's trip in 2009. Castro says the visit set the co-production negotiations in motion. In a joint statement issued during the trip, Boric and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi named audiovisual co-production among the areas where the two countries would look to work together. José Antonio Kast succeeded Boric as president in March. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories 'Narnia' White Witches Tilda Swinton and Emma Mackey Excited to Meet for the First Time at Marrakech Film Festival: 'My Absolute Dream' Claes Bang, Emma Mackey, Vicky Krieps and More Join Marion Cotillard in Marrakech Jury

"It has been started and now is at the final, final stage, so we hope that we can bring some news soon," Loyola tells Variety .

There is no firm date yet. Loyola points out that the process only began last year, adding: "We really, really hope that by next year we can announce something. If something happens earlier, more than happy, but it's a priority for Chile as well."

The treaty is moving alongside a broader trade pact, the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. The two sides finalized its terms of reference during Boric's visit and have held four rounds of talks since, the most recent in New Delhi in December 2025, according to India's embassy in Santiago. India's commerce secretary traveled to Chile in August to advance the negotiations. Bilateral trade grew from $3.84 billion in 2024 to $5.38 billion in 2025, with Indian imports of Chilean gold accounting for much of the rise. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Chilean producers are already lining up. Giancarlo Nasi, producer and CEO of Quijote Films, which operates out of Santiago and Los Angeles, came off a strong 2025. Quijote produced Diego Céspedes' "The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo," winner of the Un Certain Regard prize at Cannes, and co-produced Gabriel Mascaro's Brazilian drama "The Blue Trail," which took the Grand Jury Prize in Berlin.

"I love pushing the boundaries of what is possible and doing the craziest co-production that you can find. So co-producing with India would be ideal," Nasi says.

Without a treaty, Quijote gets around the gap by bringing in a partner from a third country that has a treaty with Chile. A French company on Ukrainian drama "Pamfir," which played Cannes in 2022, allowed Quijote to tap the Chilean-French treaty. A French company was also attached early on to John Trengove's South African drama "The Smell of Apples," which premiered at Toronto in September, and a French producer is on board the documentary Quijote is now making with Moroccan filmmaker Asmae El Moudir, who shared Cannes' documentary prize for "The Mother of All Lies" in 2023.

A direct treaty would remove that detour. Nasi says the key is for Chile to build "a minoritarian co-production fund that is bigger and bigger and stronger so it can actually make a difference for an Indian production."

A fan of Indian cinema since childhood, Nasi cites "RRR" and "The Lunchbox" as proof of its range. He has been receiving Indian projects, but has yet to find the right one. Many come from Indian filmmakers living in the U.S. who want to tell stories of migration and return, often on mid-sized budgets with no state funding available to them. He would like to make a film that spans India, the U.S. and Chile.

"There's a crisis in the States in terms of financing independent movies because the distribution system of independent movies is changing," Nasi says. "Theaters are more and more reserved to horror genre movies or big movies, so the independent dramas, they're having trouble finding a place."

Chile's factual sector is also in the hunt. The 64th FICX honorary prize was shared between two cult figures at the festival: Irish actor, writer and director Peter Mullan while a special mention went to Mexican-director Carlos Reygadas .

Mullan has a long standing relationship with Gijón after working as an actor with Ken Loach, Danny Boyle and Steven Spielberg among other. articles.title: 5 Spider-Man: The Animated Series Storylines That Deserve to Be in the MCU
articles.summary: With Spider-Man: Brand New Day as Tom Holland's fourth solo film, the Marvel Cinematic Universe has now featured more Spider-Man stories on the big screen than any previous iteration. That's the case without even mentioning his appearances in larger MCU projects alongside other heroes. The thing about Spider-Man is that he has so many great […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google With Spider-Man: Brand New Day as Tom Holland's fourth solo film, the Marvel Cinematic Universe has now featured more Spider-Man stories on the big screen than any previous iteration. That's the case without even mentioning his appearances in larger MCU projects alongside other heroes. The thing about Spider-Man is that he has so many great tales and storylines that they could keep making highly entertaining movies about him for as long as they want. A good place to look for inspiration is Spider-Man: The Animated Series from the '90s . The show has withstood the test of time as a legitimate classic superhero series.

Seeing some of the spectacular stories from the show come to life in the MCU would be incredible. However, there are some great ones that wouldn't entirely fit into the franchise. "Six Forgotten Warriors" features an odd mix of characters for the MCU, while the Man-Spider arc known as "Neogenic Nightmare" was kind of touched upon in Spider-Man: Brand New Day . There's also the Secret Wars arc that is clealry going to be part of Avengers: Secret Wars , so that's out of the question. Thankfully, Spider-Man: The Animated Series has plenty of other great stories the MCU could pull from.

Spider-Wars is the kind of story that feels ripe for adaptation in the Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse franchise but the MCU could do something fun with it too. This was the closing arc of the '90s series and it sees the main Spider-Man parnter up with several variations from the multiverse. That is basically the premise for Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse , but this one also involved characters like Madame Web and The Beyonder.

It would be interesting to see Tom Holland's Spider-Man join forces again with Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield while also throwing in a couple of other brand new variants. The MCU would also be able to introduce its own version of Madame Web after the Sony movie flopped. These Spider-Men come together to take on a Spider-Carnage variant and that's a villain who would be incredible to see on the big screen. Watching a Peter deal with a symbiote that isn't Venom sounds refreshing.

The combination of Spider-Man and Dardevil is one that just makes too much sense. Both are street-level heroes based out of New York and their personalities make for great entertainment. Spidey is more lighthearted and quippy, while Daredevil is more serious and stoic, which is a tremendous combination. The "Man Without Fear" episodes of Spider-Man: The Animated Series played into that dynamic while also involving characters like Kingpin.

Kingpin is a major antagonist for both heroes and Vincent D'Onofrio's performance as the character in the MCU makes him someone we always want more of. This story sees Kingpin's son frame Peter Parker for treason and the MCU could do the same but with just Kingpin behind it. Matt Murdock becomes Peter's lawyer, putting them on the same team both in and out of their superhero alter egos. The show also delivered a fun twist as it was J. Jonah Jameson who paid Murdock to defend Peter, which shows a different side of Jameson, though that's unlikely in an MCU adaptation.

Despite the many iterations of Spider-Man in movies over the years, Black Cat is a character who hasn't appeared to date. The closest we came was Felicity Jones as Felicia Hardy in a small part in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 , which never grew into more. Seeing someone bring Hardy to life in the MCU would be fantastic and would feel fresh, especially if the franchise is moving past the Peter and MJ relationship.

Even if they aren't, there's a lot of drama that can be pulled from Peter trying to reconnect with MJ while spending time with the increasingly flirtatious Black Cat . The "Partners in Danger" arc showcases Hardy's origin story and sees her work with Peter, despite also being an antagonist. Watching Peter grapple with being pulled towards MJ and Felicia is an intriguing dynamic to see play out, as is seeing Peter deal with the fact that Felicia is a criminal at heart.

One of the wildest things that Spider-Man: The Animated Series pulled off was reveal that Mary Jane was a clone. The character was written off for a while and returned to Peter's shock and happiness. The two got married and went on their honeymoon, which was interrupted by MJ's ex-boyfriend, Morrie Bench. Morrie had become Hydro-Man , which is a villain who would be cool to see in live-action, especially given how a similar character looked in Spider-Man: Far From Home .

The story ultimately led to Peter finding out that the Mary Jane he married is actually a clone, while the real MJ who he initially fell in love with is lost in the multiverse. The MCU adapting this would play into the multiverse stories they're telling and would mark another bit of heartbreak for Peter, which is a staple of his character. The show famously saw the cloned MJ evaporate, meaning Peter loses her once again. The love that fans have for Holland and Zendaya's takes on the characters would make this extra emotional.

Venom has been brought to the screen a lot over the years but we haven't had enough Carnage. Putting them together in the MCU for an arc from the animated series would be ideal, especially given how this story plays out. As part of the "Sins of the Father" episodes, the danger that Carnage poses to everyone forces Spider-Man and Venom to team up, which is an easy sell for the MCU since Venom is already so popular. Seeing their relationship in a different light would be a welcome sight.

This "Sins of the Father" storyline also fits for the MCU because it brought so many characters together, which we know is something the franchise loves to do. Elements of the arc involve Doctor Strange, Mordo, Dormammu, Iron Man, and War Machine. While the MCU can't make all of that happen, it would give a chance for Spider-Man to team up with Doctor Strange again, play into the abandoned Mordo storyline, and give us fresh takes on Venom and Carnage.

Are there any other storylines from Spider-Man: The Animated Series that you'd like to see in the MCU? Let us know in the comments!

EXCLUSIVE: For Fin Taylor , one half of the satirical podcast Fin Vs History , there's no going back to TV now.

The British stand-up comedian, writer and podcaster, who fronts his show with fellow comedian Horatio Gould , had over the years made appearances on staple British comedy shows such as Live at the Apollo and The Last Leg , but his deliberately shocking style didn't feel like a good fit – to him.

As we sit down for lunch at the Ham Yard Hotel in London, he recalls making a VT for BBC news satire The Mash Report that had been cut so severely that it made his deliberately anti-woke character seemed more "fascist" than a satirical take on a news reporter. He was livid. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Executives Reed Hastings On Netflix Shakeup, YouTube Rivalry And How Streamer Can Go Back To "Being Thrilling" News Sue Perkins Exploring ADHD Diagnosis For First Time In Audible Podcast 'Attention, Please! "This was during Covid, when agents weren’t allowed to come to the record," he recalls. "I went into the gallery and I threw my toys out of the pram, and said, ‘You can’t use that in the show.’ I had basically accepted I wouldn’t be asked back, but weirdly they called the next morning and apologized, and they got me to write more stuff for them." Even though that worked out, the incident was one of several that made Taylor seek out a different path. There was also a wild broadcast where he was asked to give the British perspective on NFL Network's Good Morning Football , leading to what can only be described as mayhem and the naming of his company, Fumblerooski Productions. Watch the video below for context on that.

Taylor knew that his television future would be "the funny guy on a show that's not comedy, like Sewing Bee ," but says: "They’re never going to book me to do that because I’m a bull in a China shop. They’re not putting me on The Great British Bake Off . I needed to do my own thing."

For Gould, a comedian's life as a TV star felt even more alien. "I didn’t see anything on TV that I would want to do, or would want me," he says. Both men had been active on the UK stand-up scene, but Gould, who's slightly younger than his podcast partner, natively posted his comedy online, and he was sure his future was more likely in digital self-publishing than on the BBC or ITV. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"We all looked over to America, which is always five years ahead," says Gould. "There were so many comedians doing video podcasts and shows it was only a matter of time before it came over here."

Soon Taylor, Gould and Irish comedian Vittorio Angelone had devised Fin Vs the Internet , an online comedy series vehicle for Taylor in which he would play a deluded interviewer determined to find out why those he spoke with had bigger and better online followings than he did.

"He was like a Between Two Ferns -meets-Eric Andre character, who has no idea how the internet works and has views of a man from the '50s," says Gould, who wrote and produced the show, but remained off screen. "These were people who are very careful about their brands and he was like a bulldozer," adds Taylor.

Guests included YouTube star JaackMaate, comedian and OnlyFans performer Rebecca Goodwin, reality star and podcaster Jamie Laing, and Love Island contestant Chris Williamson, whose podcast Taylor and Gould have appeared on directly before we meet. (That episode published online yesterday.) Four seasons of the show ran between 2022 and 2024, and an accompanying Patreon podcast was created.

Then a little twist of fate led to Fin Vs History . Taylor and Gould – British men who both have history degrees – had recently been to Ireland, so they decided to film themselves talking about the country's history without doing any proper research, primarily to troll Angelone, an Irish stand-up comic. "That went really well, and it was actually exciting to do," says Taylor. "Vittorio was starting a tour and we did a few more of them, and then we started realizing the clicks were going nuts."

However, it was clear even at this stage a paywalled production could not last in the long term. "The Patreon podcast didn’t really work," says Gould. "The idea was we wanted to keep giving people weekly stuff to pay for a web series that took ages to make." However, this period ended up serving as "perfect development" for what eventually launched in January 2025 as Fin Vs History .

Angelone, who had his own podcast, amicably stepped aside ("He's now our IRA correspondent," says Taylor), while Gould had to square the time drain of another production alongside his popular Boys Gone Wild video podcast show – and potentially a continuation of the Patreon podcast. The latter was scrapped and the focus went entirely on creating Fin Vs History .

Taylor's Fumblerooski Productions, which he runs with exec producer Pete Wells ("the George Martin figure," as they call him), took on production and Podmasters, the UK-based independent podcast network, signed it to help expand the audience and monetize the show.

Gould was obsessed with Brian McGee, an aged 1970s BBC presenter and philosopher who presented stuffy, hour-long TV conversations, and felt this should be the aesthetic for a comedy show satirising history academics.

"He was this very bored, ancient-looking professor of philosophy, who would just sit on a beige sofa for an hour in front of a beige background with an even older guy with an even more dandruff-flecked suit, and they would talk about Wittgenstein."

Accordingly, each episode sees Taylor and Gould sitting facing each other in ill-fitting, bunching suits or military regalia, including hats they rent from the National Theatre. "We have a whole tailoring operation," says Taylor as an aside. "The sofa means you can’t help but be in this funny position," adds Gould. "It would not be as funny if we were on a sofa in just our trackies." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

Taylor and Gould take on the personas of two out-of-touch history buffs with extremely questionable views on almost every issue and every part of history, often taking the side of the very worst people and views in human history. "'Hitler: Friend of the pod' is the fundamental joke," says Gould, explaining their characters' warped worldviews.

Fin Vs History is deliberately provocative and certainly shocking to the unsuspecting listeners – and some have called the podcast right-leaning, though its creators say it is a staunchly non-political show and purely there to find the next laugh. "It is about doing everything you shouldn’t do, whilst dressed as if you really care about it," explains Taylor. "I trust that if you don’t find that funny, you just won’t listen to it. If you listen to the episodes, it is genuinely impossible not to understand that nothing in it is sincere."

"That’s what’s great about internet TV," adds Gould. "Back in the day, you would go into someone’s home and you had certain responsibilities and had to cater to the audience. We are in a corner of the internet putting our stuff out."

"We’re in an old lawn bowls club in Anerley. Why are you here?" quips Taylor, slipping effortlessly into his curmudgeonly character.

Since launching in early 2025, Fin Vs History has exploded in popularity, surpassing 66 million downloads with deep-dive series on the likes of Horatio Nelson, pirates, Roman Emperors, the Russian revolution, the Nazis and World War II, Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and, more quirkily, a much-loved episode on the 2018 Thai cave rescue. It won a Chortle Award, sold put the O2 Shepherd's Bush Empire with a live show and was nominated for Best Comedy Podcast at the British Podcast Awards.

On Spotify, it currently ranks as the 12th most-popular video podcast in the UK, behind the likes of The Rest is History , on which the show shares topical DNA, and The Joe Rogan Experience . Serendipity played a part there: The show began booming just as music service Spotify went all-out on video podcasting to compete with YouTube. "Because we started doing well, they started to push us more as their success story," says Taylor. "We did get lucky on the timing."

" Fin vs History is exactly the kind of show we love at Podmasters," Martin Bojtos, co-founder and CEO of Podmasters upon re-signing the pod in September. "It is original, fearless and completely distinctive. To see it grow at this speed has been incredible, but what means just as much is that Fin, Horatio and the team have chosen to continue that journey with us. For us, that trust is a real measure of success."

The show has nearly 60,000 paying Patreon subscribers (playfully known as "losers"), who get early access and exclusive content – a long running podcast in-joke is this is a bigger membership than the terrorist organization ISIS.

"I always had the sense I wanted to be funded by lots of people paying little things rather than one brand paying a lot," says Gould of the business model. "It means you can do what you want. Piss off one person, that’s £3 [$3.90]." Taylor finishes his thought: "Piss off one brand, £10,000."

Gould does worry that the exponential growth towards a more mainstream audience could lead to the nuance of the underlying joke of Fin Vs History being lost, but Taylor takes a different view – there will be a ceiling to the audience.

"It was never supposed to be mainstream in the way we’re talking about stuff," he says. "We’re always going to be in The Rest is History ’s shadow because that is mainstream. The Rest is History is so big that you can subvert it and still be one of the biggest podcasts in the country. I genuinely think if you come to Fin Vs History not knowing why it’s funny, you don’t find it funny." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

The Fin vs History podcast, via Taylor's Fumblerooski, and Gould are separately both represented by CAA, which has been heavily pushing into the creator space in the UK since last year, as we reported back in December 2025 . Gould is also managed by 42 for film and TV.

They share an agent, Glenn Miller, whose team are seeking to expand the brand – CAA's Harriet Pollard led a five-way auction for Taylor's debut book, The History of Mankind in its Entirety , earlier this year. The satirical book, written in the same voice as Taylor's podcast version of himself, published in September.

"CAA basically seeks to exploit the IP we make," says Taylor. "They’re always looking for opportunities with the streamers for podcasts. The old way felt you couldn’t start anything because the ratings had to be part of it from the start, and now we’re just doing what we want, and the agent might say, ‘Hey, I can do X to your earnings.’ For me, that’s a much better way round where it still feels like it’s me, but there’s someone there maximizing it."

The future for the podcast includes animation, which it has experimented with in some episodes. "We have long-term animation ambitions, and we’re building out that side of it," says Taylor, who adds: "The writing team we’re a part of and have accumulated would be perfect for an animated sitcom, which [British] TV was never able to do."

"The key is being able to turn something around with no red tape, basically," adds Gould. "That’s why South Park works so well. They’ve got this production line that feels so free."

Gould says there have been discussions for a travel-themed Fin Vs offshoot, and is open to "any medium we can turn this show into," while Taylor says new productions would be contingent on Fumblerookski continuing to build. "I only want to do certain topics when our animation capabilities are ready," he explains. "Video podcasting is so new and the resources are coming in."

As our lunch at Ham Yard comes to a close, the conversation turns back to the nature of traditional broadcasting. Taylor recalls a BBC radio appearance that left him cold, and says Fin Vs History has proven he only wants to engage in projects in which he makes executive decisions, while Gould says the video podcast "is TV now," and that the medium "can be anything – we used to open with sketches, just to experiment."

Taylor believes Fin Vs History represents "the perfect vehicle for creativity as comics who love history, and adds: "I just want it to keep being creative and not to feel like it’s becoming formulaic and stale, and I like the idea there will be another show borne out of this one. What’s nice is it’s all down to us."

For Taylor and Gould, TV is more likely on their list of historical subjects to cover than a pathway for the future.

articles.title: Home Alone's Most Misunderstood Moment Isn't a Plot Hole, But It's Easy to Miss
articles.summary: As the end of the year approaches, people start getting ready for Christmas and all the traditions that come with it. One of the most popular ones is rewatching holiday movies, and, of course, Home Alone is pretty much guaranteed to make the list. The '90s classic that became a franchise and is now reportedly […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google As the end of the year approaches, people start getting ready for Christmas and all the traditions that come with it. One of the most popular ones is rewatching holiday movies , and, of course, Home Alone is pretty much guaranteed to make the list. The '90s classic that became a franchise and is now reportedly getting another sequel with Macaulay Culkin has entertained generations of viewers, but despite its popularity, it still raises a pretty big question. The whole premise revolves around Kevin being left home alone while his family travels to Paris for Christmas, but you've probably wondered how the McCallisters managed to fly to another country without realizing they'd left an eight-year-old child behind.

It's a ridiculous situation when you actually stop to think about it , after all, we're talking about a kid, not a suitcase that someone could accidentally forget in all the holiday chaos. And that's why some people have come to consider this a plot hole, assuming it's just something the movie expects audiences to overlook so they can enjoy the story. But here's the thing: there's actually a scene that answers this question and makes it way easier to understand everything. The problem is that it happens very quickly, right in the middle of a chaotic moment, which makes it also easy to miss.

Early in the movie, we see the McCallister family getting ready for their trip, and the house is in a complete mess: relatives are arriving, everyone is busy packing and making last-minute preparations, and Kevin is having trouble getting along with his brother, Buzz (Devin Ratray). During dinner, he teases the protagonist about a cheese pizza, and Kevin doesn't take the jokes so well. Because of that, he lunges at his brother, and the two end up causing quite a scene in the kitchen. In the process, milk gets spilled all over the table, soaking some of the important documents, including their passports and plane tickets.

Peter (John Heard), the family patriarch, tries to clean up the mess but accidentally makes things worse without realizing it. In the middle of all the commotion, while gathering the wet napkins and cleaning the table, he also picks up Kevin's plane ticket and throws it in the trash. The camera briefly shows the ticket inside the garbage can, with the boy's name visible, before more napkins cover it. The shot lasts less than a second, and because you're focused on the argument and all the chaos surrounding it, you can easily overlook. There's also no reaction from anyone to suggest that Peter has just made a mistake, so the movie simply moves on. You can see it at the 2:51 mark in the video:

And that little mistake Peter makes is relevant the following morning. During the night, a storm causes a power outage, resetting the house's alarm clocks. Therefore, the McCallisters oversleep and go into full panic mode as they try to make it to the airport on time. Kevin, who was sent to sleep in the attic after his fight with Buzz, is still asleep while everyone else gets ready to leave. And, of course, with so many people rushing around the house , nobody notices that he's missing. And when Heather (Kristin Minter), one of Kevin's cousins, counts all the children before they get into the van, she accidentally includes a neighborhood boy who happens to be standing nearby with his back turned.

Now, imagine if Kevin's ticket had still been with the other documents. Even if nobody noticed he was missing during the rush to leave the house, someone could have spotted an extra one when the family arrived at the airport, right? It would be natural to check everyone's tickets before boarding and wonder why there was one for a child who wasn't there. But overall, the whole film isn't trying to be all that realistic either, and it uses several convenient coincidences to get Kevin home alone—and some of the cast members have actually discussed just how questionable this setup is.

The difficulty of buying into the Home Alone 's premise isn't just something audiences started complaining about years later, as Heard acknowledged that the situation wasn't exactly easy to believe. In an interview with EDGE Magazine , the actor was asked how a family could board a plane to Europe without noticing they'd left one of their children behind. He revealed that both he and Catherine O'Hara (who played Kate, the family's mother) had their own doubts about the situation and weren't entirely sure how to approach it:

"Between the two of us, she had the more difficult part. I could just be sort of a dummy, a goofy guy—I made him a gynecologist—I didn’t care, as long as she was as focused as she was in terms of losing our son," he explained. However, things became confusing when they found out what kind of movie they were making. "Then we learned that it was a comedy. Why is this funny? How do we play this? We didn’t really know how comedic all that slapstick stuff was going to be until we saw it. It wasn’t until the second Home Alone that we knew that we could be funny."

So, all in all, the moment when Kevin's plane ticket gets thrown away isn't exactly a new discovery. Still, it's a detail that keeps on surprising most people, especially during the holiday season, when the film gets another round of rewatches . Is it a convenient chain of events? Sure, but at least it makes for a pretty entertaining comedy. Home Alone is a classic after all.

Home Alone is available to stream on Disney+.

articles.title: 4 Years Ago, Star Wars Scrapped Its First-Ever "F-Bomb" And It Would Have Been Perfect
articles.summary: Star Wars has been struggling since the Disney purchase of Lucasfilm, but it's not really as bad as everyone likes to say. The sequel trilogy gets a lot of hate, but most of it comes from people who didn't like a girl hero to be put over their childhood favorites. While there are definitely legitimate […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Star Wars has been struggling since the Disney purchase of Lucasfilm, but it's not really as bad as everyone likes to say. The sequel trilogy gets a lot of hate, but most of it comes from people who didn't like a girl hero to be put over their childhood favorites. While there are definitely legitimate things to dislike, you don't hear about them nearly as much. Star Wars animation has been incredible since Disney+ first started making shows, with the final season of Star Wars: The Clone Wars, The Bad Batch, Star Wars Visions, the various Tales shows, The Ninth Jedi , and the rest impressing. Even on the live-action front, things are better than most people want to admit (I am still salty about people's reaction to The Acolyte ), with one show rising far above anything in Star Wars ever. However, the original plan would have made this masterpiece legitimately groundbreaking.

Star Wars: Andor was a prequel to Rogue One: A Star Wars Story . While that movie is probably the most praised of Disney's tenure (although, The Last Jedi is actually the better movie, come at me in the comments), fans didn't really know what to expect from Andor . Most figured at best it would be about the same level as the movie, possibly a little worse. We didn't really expect Tony Gilroy and company to blow us away like the Death Star on Scariff. The show took things in a more mature direction, using the setting of the pre- A New Hope era to tell a story about fascism and how it affects everyone. However, there was a chance it could have been way mature, as Tony Gilroy has talked about the things Disney didn't let him say , including Maarva Andor dropping a certain F-shaped bomb in the greatest Star Wars scene of all-time.

So, going back to A New Hope , one of the things that appealed to fans so much about Star Wars was that it wasn't "pretty" sci-fi. This wasn't the Enterprise , with its spacious crew quarters and rounded off lines, the universe of Star Wars was gritty and jagged, with a lived-in quality that made it all seem real. The prequels changed that, as the Republic was more high tech and clean, but Andor brought it back. Most of the first season took place on Ferrix, a small colony world out on the periphery, a world where scrapping Clone Wars-era tech paid the bills.

Andor was a story about how the various social classes deal with fascism. Cassian, Bix, Brasso, Wilmon, and Maarva were in the lowest class, having to deal with a social system where they had no rights or power. There was a sense of tension throughout the first season (I mean, through the show in general, but it was one of the key parts of the first season's narrative), as everyone was pushed closer and closer to the breaking point by the circumstances of the galaxy. Maarva's funeral was an orgiastic moment of release for our main characters and the people of Ferrix, and it's one of the reasons the first season is so beloved.

Andor Season One was like communist theory, in a lot of ways, showing you why the system of the Empire was bad. A lot of people talk about The Trail of Political Consciousness , the anti-Imperial manifesto written by Karis Nemik, but the first season is basically his manifesto in macrocosm and it's why the F-bomb would have been perfect. "F-k the Empire" would have been the perfect way to illustrate where the characters were.

Andor was a lot like old Star Wars Legends , using ideas from the West End Games sourcebooks (I still have a bunch of those; they're great lore companions for Legends). One of the interesting thing about Legends is that the creators came up with their own curse words. The F-word equivalent was usually "kriff". The canon Expanded Universe does still use them and they are fun little Easter Eggs for people like me, who read all of that stuff when they were teenager. However, they never would have got the point across because only the diehards know them.

Adding the "F-k the Empire," line to Andor Season One would have been the perfect way to show how much pressure and stress everyone was under. The first season – and the show in general – worked so well because it was able to create this flawless atmosphere of tension; adding this line to the season would have worked out so well for several reasons

To begin with, it's never been done in Star Wars and it would get an immediate attention. You can look at like this – even if this is the first time we've heard that word, that means it does exist but it's one of the worst things you can say, and they could have played it like a certain curse word that is used a lot in Great Britain and Australia, but you can't say in the United States. We talk about a lot about "aura" and "vibes" in the 2020s, and the F-bomb's use in Andor would have had unassailable aura and immaculate vibes (I'm too old to say that, aren't I?).

It also would have another affect, something that show already did so well – make the audience understand how the characters felt. Andor wouldn't have been nearly as successful without its ability to connect the audience with the struggle onscreen . Having Maarva end her funeral speech with, "F-k the Empire!" would have made the scene that much more powerful because we've all been there. We've all been in that place where staying polite in the face of monstrous injustice is just too much and you need to get it out. That's what we could have had and it would have been glorious.

There are few scenes in Star Wars history as good as Maarva Andor's funeral. Even pulling back from its place in the story, it was a perfectly set-up, choreographed, acted, and shot scene. It was an example of everyone in the cast and crew putting their best work forward. It's a scene that still gives people goosebumps four years later. The only way it would have been better is if Maarva Andor got to end her speech with a posthumous F-bomb.

Star Wars has often struggled with how it is perceived. On the one hand, some of its original diehard fans are on Social Security right now, or about to be, and they've stayed with it all these years because there is a certain maturity to the franchise that still appeals to them. However, it's also a franchise where the creator was able to buy back the film rights because of toy sales. It has always had a little something for everybody; the younger fans got stuff like Star Wars Visions and The Ninth Jedi (anime is all the rage with the kids, he says, as he rubs his aching back) and the older fans got stuff like Andor (some of them will say the same about Revenge of the Sith , but that's because they were 8 when they first watched it and it felt dark and mature to them; it's just like my generation with Return of the Jedi ).

Putting the F-bomb in Andor would have a great moment. It definitely fit the show's tone and would have been an amazing moment that broke new ground in Star Wars . It also would do the one thing that the creators had done so well across the length of the show – further build the world of the show, making it more real. Honestly, I don't think really think there will ever be a more perfect moment to bring the F-bomb to the galaxy far, far away than this one. It was a missed opportunity.

What do you think about Andor potentially using the F-bomb? Do you think it would have fit the world or do you think Disney was right to leave it out? Sound off in the comment section below.

The film centers on Hina, a Kashmiri refugee who is convicted of murdering her husband. At the open prison, where inmates are permitted to leave during the day to work in the city but must return by 6 p.m. for roll call, she finds support and companionship in fellow prisoner Dharam. The two fall in love, but Dharam is consumed by guilt over a crime he committed 15 years earlier. His attempts at redemption include obsessively donating blood. When Hina discovers his past, she struggles to forgive him, even as she hopes the world will forgive her. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories UFC's Event Sellout Spree Powers TKO Q3 Earnings WWE, Disney Team for 'Avengers: Doomsday'-Themed Worlds Collide, John Cena Classic

"In most prison films, we see stories of escape and punishment. But in this prison story, the driving force is love," says Saxena, who co-wrote the screenplay with Ram Kumar Singh, a fellow Jaipur native familiar with the prison and its inmates.

The idea has its roots in Saxena's childhood. An open prison in the middle of her city first introduced her to the concepts of rehabilitation and reintegration. Later, reading Dostoevsky's "Crime and Punishment" and Victor Hugo's "Les Misérables" deepened her interest in the relationship between crime, punishment and human change.

"I hope audiences leave asking what they would do in Hina's place, and whether a sentence ever truly ends for the person who served it," she says.

Saxena, an alumna of the Film and Television Institute of India, made her feature debut with "Sad Letters of an Imaginary Woman," which premiered at the Busan International Film Festival in 2024 and received the festival's Asian Cinema Fund post-production support. "I didn't even know about the concept of an open prison before. And on top of that, it was a love story between two prisoners," says producer Naren Kumar of Mumbai-based Kyra Kumar Kreations, whose credits include co-producing the "Jolly LLB" films and producing the series "Maharani" (SonyLIV). "I was drawn to a love story that refuses easy forgiveness, to two characters asking what a person owes the world after paying for what they've done."

articles.summary: Ayan Mukerji, director of the Ranbir Kapoor-starring fantasy epic "Brahmastra: Part One – Shiva," told audiences at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa that his next creative focus is the sequel, "Brahmastra 2." articles.content:
Ayan Mukerji , director of the Ranbir Kapoor -starring fantasy epic "Brahmastra: Part One – Shiva," told audiences at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa that his next creative focus is the sequel, "Brahmastra 2."

"I hope that we can make 'Brahmastra 2' even more Indian," Mukerji said, adding that he hoped to draw more deeply from Indian mythology this time.

Mukerji was in conversation with Basil Joseph, the director of Malayalam-language superhero film "Minnal Murali," at a session titled "The Epic Genres – Mythologies, Superheroes & New Worlds," where the two made the case for homegrown fantasy franchises. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Here's How to Watch WWE Crown Jewel 2026 Live Online WWE, Disney Team for 'Avengers: Doomsday'-Themed Worlds Collide, John Cena Classic

"We have our own heroes which we call gods," Joseph said when asked what makes Indian fantasy distinct. The West, he said, wrote its superheroes into comics, and he linked the genre's pull to hope. "The storytelling has always been around," said Mukerji, pointing to Indian television, adding that vast territory remains untouched on the big screen.

Mukerji credited advances in VFX with making such projects feel feasible. Joseph had little time for AI as a creative shortcut. "AI is not creating anything new; it's reproducing," he said, predicting that the future will be "all about originality."

"I was discovering the kind of film I was trying to make," Mukerji said of "Brahmastra," the Hindi-language fantasy released in 2022 with Kapoor as Shiva. The film started life as "a slightly more intimate coming-of-age film" called "Dragon" before growing in budget, effects work and scope. "Some people liked the film, some people didn't. But the audience is very smart and you have to respect their reaction even if it doesn't go in your favor," he said. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Looking back, Mukerji said that spending so much time with "Brahmastra" in post-production had led him to cut scenes and actors' pauses too sharply for the theatrical release. He later restored some of them in the streaming version. "Overthinking is not always improving," he said.

Joseph made "Minnal Murali," set in the fictional village of Kurukkanmoola, within the budget of a Malayalam-language production. He pointed to the look of protagonist Jaison (Tovino Thomas), drawn from the rural Kerala milieu, and a scarecrow face standing in for a villain's disguise. "All these ideas came from that restriction," he said. Unable to lean on heavy VFX, his team chose to "get the basics right," betting that a strong script would carry the film even where the effects fell short. "The restrictions made the film more innovative," he said.

In hindsight, Joseph said, "I got a little carried away with the villain of that film." He cautioned that filmmakers building new worlds "get too ambitious" and "overpack everything." His advice was to "keep it simple, be original and don't try too hard to look cool."

"Minnal Murali" was made for theaters, Joseph said, but the pandemic and theater closures led to its release on Netflix. "Everything happens for a reason," he said, adding that while a sequel was planned if the film worked, for now he was busy with a different project.

During the audience Q&A, Mukerji was asked to choose between Kapoor as Shiva in "Brahmastra" and as Rama in "Ramayana." He picked Rama.

The session closed on a note of mutual admiration, with Mukerji joking, "I'll give Basil my next script to read and take some notes from him," and Joseph responding, "I'll give you mine."

Best Friend Forever has closed new sales deals for " Elephants in the Fog " in Mexico, South Korea and Portugal, as Nepal's Oscar entry for best international feature film builds a campaign around impact screenings that place the Kinnar community it portrays at the center of policy conversations.

Tulip will distribute in Mexico, Film Dabin in South Korea and Leopardo Filmes in Portugal. Talks for North American rights are under way. The new deals bring the film's total to 17 territories, following earlier agreements covering the U.K., Spain, Benelux, Switzerland, Israel, Australia, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, France, Germany and Austria, Brazil, Nepal and inflight rights with Silk Route. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Here's How to Watch WWE Crown Jewel 2026 Live Online WWE, Disney Team for 'Avengers: Doomsday'-Themed Worlds Collide, John Cena Classic

The campaign's most recent stop was U.N. Headquarters in New York, where the film screened on Nov. 20 – Transgender Day of Remembrance. The event was co-hosted by the Permanent Missions of Nepal, Norway, France and Brazil to the United Nations, together with Outright International. Gyan Bahadur Magar, Nepal's Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations, opened the evening by honoring those killed for their identity and paying tribute to community organizations including Blue Diamond Society, Nepal's leading LGBTIQ+ rights organization, for their response to the country's August floods despite severe resource constraints. "LGBTIQ+ persons must be partners in shaping decisions, not merely beneficiaries of policies," he said. "Remembrance without action is not enough. Recognition without protection is not enough."

Lead actress Pushpa Thing Lama – an activist with Blue Diamond Society since 2005 – addressed the room in a video message. The panel that followed, "Leaving No One Behind: Including LGBTI People in Humanitarian Response," featured Anjali Lama, Nepal's first transgender model; Vivek Rai, deputy director of the Civil Society Division at UN Women; André du Plessis, U.N. program director of Outright International; and Ana Seco Díaz, the film's impact producer. Du Plessis said trans people are too often discussed at the United Nations and in politics as an ideology, making it all the more important to put real people in front of those debates. "Inclusion is not charity. It is a matter of human rights," said Anjali Lama. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The screening connected the film to a broader humanitarian argument. When floods and landslides struck Nepal in August, 987 people were killed and 3,916 left missing, and the country's gender and sexual minority communities found that legal protections on the books did not reliably carry through into emergency response. A report presented to the General Assembly last month by Graeme Reid, the U.N. Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, found that LGBT people face compounding exclusion during humanitarian crises. Reid said that trans people are too often invisible in emergency systems, and that the people most affected by a crisis must be part of shaping the response to it. Following cuts to USAID, Blue Diamond Society laid off 262 of its 350 staff and was forced to close 21 of its clinics.

"If the film clears even a little of the fog of prejudice, allowing someone to truly see another person, or perhaps even a part of themselves, then I feel the work has done something meaningful," director Abinash Bikram Shah said.

The campaign continues on Dec. 1 – World AIDS Day – in London at the Arzner, the U.K.'s LGBTQ+ cinema, in partnership with the Terrence Higgins Trust and Amnesty U.K.'s Queer Rights Network, with funds raised going to the Trust and to Blue Diamond Society. Members of Parliament have been invited to hear how cuts to international aid have hit community-led organizations like Blue Diamond Society. On Dec. 3, Film Independent takes the film to Los Angeles for its Programmers' Picks series.

The Cannes Un Certain Regard Jury Prize winner is Nepal's submission in this year's Oscar international feature race. Since its Cannes premiere it has also won the Grand Jury Prize at NewFest. Pushpa Thing Lama received the best performance prize at the Asia Pacific Screen Awards. In France, the film has surpassed 80,000 admissions, an unprecedented figure for a Nepali release.

"Elephants in the Fog" is directed by Abinash Bikram Shah, whose short "Lori" received a Special Mention at the Cannes Short Film Competition in 2022. articles.summary: India is poised for its highest box office since the pandemic, provided the remaining weeks of 2026 go as expected, Girish Johar, head of distribution and revenues at Zee Studios, said at WAVES Film Bazaar, the market held alongside the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. articles.content:
India is poised for its highest box office since the pandemic, provided the remaining weeks of 2026 go as expected, Girish Johar, head of distribution and revenues at Zee Studios, said at WAVES Film Bazaar , the market held alongside the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

Johar was speaking on a panel titled "One Film, Multiple Paydays: Extracting a Film's Full Value," which looked at the changing economics of filmmaking, the value of intellectual property (IP) and the need to find audiences across platforms. Moderated by producer Vikramjit Roy, the panel also featured Ashish Saksena, COO of cinemas at BookMyShow, India's leading ticketing platform; Aashish Singh, producer at Shah Rukh Khan's Red Chillies Entertainment; and Esther Li, producer at Hong Kong-based Mirage Films. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Tallinn Takeaways: Buzz Titles, the Baltics’ Build and Freedom of Speach Under Pressure Sandra Hüller To Be Honored With Spotlight Award At Palm Springs International Film Awards (EXCLUSIVE)

For Singh, IP stands for intellectual property, but in his head it is like an insurance policy. "So your intellectual property is actually your insurance policy for the future," he said. "If you get it right, it can pay you through the years and pay your future generations."

Singh acknowledged that producers typically acquire IP through buy-outs because they assume the financial risk, but said ownership and revenue-sharing were matters for negotiation. He advised writers to register their work with the Screenwriters Association (SWA).

Studios aim to recover 60% to 70% of a film's budget through pre-sales, Singh said. "The pre-sales may not happen immediately, but over a period of time, with a certain star, with a certain genre of the film, you may be able to recover money through OTT [streaming], satellite, and music," he said, adding that satellite sales had become challenging. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Saksena said BookMyShow shares audience insights and market intelligence with producers, helping them see where a film is finding traction and where further marketing may be needed. "We don't like to think of a movie as a one-off, just being online for a short time," he said. He encouraged independent filmmakers to consider transactional video-on-demand (TVOD) through BookMyShow Stream, as well as screening slots at the company's Red Lorry Film Festival. "You cannot pitch every film to everyone in India. You have to be very segmented and targeted," he said.

Offering an international perspective, Li cited the success in China of Indian films such as Aamir Khan's wrestling drama "Dangal" and Vijay Sethupathi starrer "Maharaja." She said Chinese audiences appreciated their social concerns, inspirational qualities and distinctive humor. "The love stories in Indian films are really romantic," she said, describing the emotional experience of watching them in theaters as part of the appeal.

Li advised independent filmmakers to develop a distinctive creative identity, with a unique voice, visual style and film language, while making sure audiences could relate to the emotions in their work.

Speakers noted that Indian cinema was still waiting for an international breakout on the scale of Bong Joon Ho's "Parasite," the 2019 Korean film that went on to win the best picture Oscar, which could open up new markets.

Johar said the choice between a theatrical and a streaming release depended on the filmmaker's point of view, the content and the budget. "Audiences are loyal to content, IP, and characters," he said, adding that stars were no longer the key factor in a film's success. When small films want to get into the limelight, Johar said, "they want to scale from 200 screens to 1,000 screens, which can kill the film."

He suggested that streaming fatigue had helped lift box office in India. "At the end of the day, we all want a social gathering, we all want to watch movies on the big screen," Johar said. "And if we give audiences stories which are relatable, which is what we are seeing, then we also see a huge upswing in box office."
