"For me, this is like returning home. The essence of Hindustani classical. The essence of India," Rahman said. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Dakota Johnson to Star and Produce Relationship Dramedy 'Tell Me Everything' for Lionsgate Marvel’s ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Won’t Screen for BAFTA, Golden Globes and Other Early Awards Groups to Guard Its Spoilers (EXCLUSIVE)

Written by Ravinder Randhawa and Sriram Rajan, "Banaras" centers on a father living with dementia and his two estranged children (Abhishek Banerjee and Shahana Goswami), who set out on a journey to confront their family history and the musical legacy they stand to inherit. The film is set against the backdrop of the Maha Kumbh Mela in Prayagraj, a Hindu pilgrimage often described as the largest gathering of people on Earth.

Rahman worked with classical vocalist Ajoy Chakrabarty and singers Vaishali Samant and Ronkini Gupta. He said restraint, ambience and silence mattered as much as the music itself.

The score came together fast. Bala approached Rahman in November, just two to three months before the Maha Kumbh began, leaving little time to develop the story, cast the film and compose its music. "They say Ganga flows. We started flowing," Bala said.

The pairing goes back decades. "Banaras," Bala's first feature since "Maryan" (2013), extends a collaboration with Rahman that includes "Vande Mataram" (1997), "Jana Gana Mana" (2000) and "Jiyo Utho Badho Jeeto," the anthem for the 2010 Commonwealth Games. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Music shaped the images too. The film was shot between Banaras (Varanasi) and Prayagraj, and cinematographer Marc Koninckx had to contend with the unpredictable Maha Kumbh crowds at the Prayagraj site. He set out to capture emotion through light, framing and composition so that audiences feel part of the action rather than observers. "The camera is like music," he said, explaining that he builds visual rhythm by setting colors and visual elements against each other.

For Neeraj Kabi, the role was a gift for an actor. "When you go into a particular space, that space takes over and everything starts happening," he said of filming at the actual Maha Kumbh. Banerjee said he drew on his own relationship with his father for the film's emotionally charged father-son confrontation, while Chhaya Kadam, who spoke about the need to understand people living with dementia, said: "Whatever is inside, should be said on time."

The film's first notes belong to another Banaras musician. Bala opens "Banaras" with archival footage of shehnai maestro Bismillah Khan, which reached him as a WhatsApp forward. "I've always missed filming him," Bala said, adding that he wanted the film to begin with "the son of the soil from Banaras."

Indian filmmaker Sreemoyee Singh's personal documentary " Fireflowers ," about a mother who lost her singing voice after her husband died, has added Dutch outfit New Amsterdam Film Company, through Sander Verdonk, as co-producer.

The project is also among the selections at this year's WAVES Film Bazaar , the market component of the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

The co-production was finalized ahead of the market. "Fireflowers" is Singh's follow-up to "And, Towards Happy Alleys," her debut documentary, which she shot in Iran and which world premiered in the Berlinale's Panorama strand in 2023. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Byron Allen's BuzzFeed Hires Chris Poydenis, Co-Founder of Creator Marketing Agency Influential, as Chief Revenue Officer Is Vanity Fair’s Hit Piece on Taylor Swift Really Journalism?

The new film turns to Singh's own family. Her parents used to sing together, and within a year of her father's death, her mother could no longer sing. Singh began training in vocal music around the same time. The film moves between her father's 1980s Calcutta and the present day, as mother and daughter work through grief that was never fully dealt with, in a city that is itself losing much of its old character. Animation is by Bob and Bobby.

"This is a story I have been born into, lived and grown with. Finally I feel ready to share it. I filmed my debut documentary in Iran, but here I turn the lens inward – into my home, and tell the story of my parents and the city I have grown up in," says Singh.

"In 'Fireflowers,' Sreemoyee Singh brings together her mother's lost voice, her father's absence and a disappearing Calcutta [Kolkata] in one intimate film. Triparna Banerjee and Singh produce for Happy Alley Films, with Dibya Chatterjee and Indraprasad Ghatak of HandyKraft Pictures also co-producing. The project was earlier pitched at DocEdge Kolkata and has received support from South Korea's DMZ Docs.

"'Fireflowers' is a mother and a daughter reflecting on grief, memory and the fragility of voice, held together by music and the city of Calcutta [Kolkata]. Producing it is my quiet resistance to the expectation that documentaries from India or South Asia must be boxed into social issues," says Banerjee.

articles.title: Obsession Just Opened the Door to An Entire Horror Franchise, And They Better Make the Most of It
articles.summary: Obsession's premiere on Netflix has continued the horror film's milestone run in 2026. After becoming a breakout phenomenon, Obsession had an impressive theatrical run ($524 million against a budget of less than $1 million) that was sustained almost entirely by word-of-mouth, and has since topped streaming charts after premiering on digital platforms, then Universal's Peacock […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Obsession 's premiere on Netflix has continued the horror film's milestone run in 2026. After becoming a breakout phenomenon, Obsession had an impressive theatrical run ($524 million against a budget of less than $1 million) that was sustained almost entirely by word-of-mouth, and has since topped streaming charts after premiering on digital platforms, then Universal's Peacock platform, and now Netflix.

With that kind of success, it shouldn't be surprising that there is already talk of writer/director Curry Barker working on a sequel . However, in the era of turning breakout films into franchise IPs, we'd be remiss to look at Obsession and not see the potential franchise-starter that it really is. In fact, the film opens such a big window of opportunity that Barker and Co. would be foolish not to seize it while it's right in front of them.

One of Obsession 's greatest achievements as an indie horror film is spooning in just the right amount contextual lore to make the core story work. The film hinges on Bear Bailey (Michael Johnsto) successfully using the "One Wish Willow" sold at a local cyrstal shop to make his crush Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette) love him. The film never gets too booged down explaining why the novelty item is actually magical, and even doubles-down on the unexplained mystery by featuring a haunting scene where Bear speaks with a customer sevice representative from One Wish WIllow on the phone. The rep clearly understands how real mysteical objects are, and how precarious the wishes can be. The rep also clearly understands that it's some entity possessing Nikki and not the real person Bear is interacting with, as he has the ability to channel the real Nikki's voice (screaming in horror) over the phone cal.

Bear quickly hangs up the call at the point, but our minds haven't stopped working: Who is One Wish Willow's customer service rep, and how does he have so much mystical insight? Obsession also teases that the company sells several mystical novelties, and generally seems like a company of supernatural curiosities. That's an idea that can be mined to create an entire Obsession universe, which would explore what other novelties from the One Wish Willow company, and the cursed effects they unleash on unsuspecting customers. And if you don't think a horror movie franchise based on a collection of supernatural curiosities is a concept that can work, you clearly haven't been paying attention to the genre.

In 2013, filmmaker James Wan made a classic haunted house horror movie called The Conjuring , based on the cases of real-life demonologist/exorcist couple, Ed and Lorraine Warren. The film cost just $20 million and ended up making nearly $320 million at the box office. Wan and the producers (including former DC Studios head Peter Safran) took just one small part of that world (Ed and Lorraine's room of cursed or possessed objects like the Annabelle doll) and blew it out into an entire franchise universe which is now 10-films strong and still counting, with a prequel film on the way .

Not only did multiple artifiacts from Ed and Lorraine's office get spun off into their own films, but those spinoffs turned into their own franchises, with Annabelle getting an entire trilogy, The Nun getting two films, while the main Conjuring series remained the Avengers of the franchise during its four-flm run, drawing the fanbase back for each of the next major chapters in Ed and Lorraine's life and career together, and the overarching prophecy of doom they had to contend with.

If it worked with The Conjuring, you can bet that it will work just as well with Obsession and its lore. The series should follow suit exactly: put out a sequel film (especially one that deals with Nikki's fate after the first film) and make sure it opens a full door to spinoffs. All that requires is a bit more investigation and reveals about the One Wish Willow company and its employees; just one scene or sequence would do the job.

Do you want to see Obsession expand into a bigger horror universe? Let us know your ideas in the comments!

articles.title: Is Robert Pattinson Done As Batman After Part 2? New Update Signals An Early End to the Reevesverse
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Warner Bros. With Robert Pattinson signed on to play the next James Bond, it appears that his time as Batman is coming to an early end. The next Batman movie from Matt Reeves has been in the works for years, and it was supposed to be the second movie in a planned trilogy. However, The Batman: Part […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google With Robert Pattinson signed on to play the next James Bond, it appears that his time as Batman is coming to an early end. The next Batman movie from Matt Reeves has been in the works for years, and it was supposed to be the second movie in a planned trilogy. However, The Batman: Part II has been constantly delayed, and it has missed several previously announced release dates. It isn't expected to arrive until February 2028. That is looking to be the last time that anyone will see Pattinson in the role of Batman, and will also mark the end of Matt Reeves' run on the title.

According to scooper Jeff Sneider, The Batman: Part II will not only be the last movie in which Robert Pattinson will play Batman, but will also be the last movie in Matt Reeves' run on the franchise. This means that the rumors that Skydance wanted Pattinson to join the DCU as Batman won't come true either.

Robert Pattinson's run as Batman is reportedly expected to end after THE BATMAN: PART 2. It's also shaping up to be Matt Reeves' final entry. 🦇 (Via @insneider) pic.twitter.com/ECrkj7D79C

The second that Robert Pattinson was cast as James Bond , it was only a matter of time before he left the Batman franchise. Pattinson is a great actor, but carrying two major roles like Batman and James Bond was likely too much to ask. When Pattinson agreed to read for the role of Bond, it was clear that he was looking for his future after Batman. Pattinson starred as Batman in 2022, and it will have been six years by the time The Batman: Part II followed it in theaters. That gave Pattinson plenty of time to work on other projects in the meantime, including The Drama , The Odyssey , and Primetime in 2026 alone.

However, Pattinson will likely have to dedicate a lot of time to his new role as James Bond, and there is no way that franchise will have the giant gaps that Matt Reeves' Batman movies had. There were rumors that David Ellison and Skydance wanted Pattinson to join the new DC movies as Batman , making the jump from Reeves' universe into the mainline DC universe, but that isn't going to happen if these new rumors of Pattinson leaving are true. It also seems that Reeves won't be finishing his trilogy, which is for the better, with all the delays on the second movie keeping the DCU from ever introducing its Batman before James Gunn's exit.

Cosmic Book News reported that Skydance sources told them Robert Pattinson was never going to remain on as Batman without Matt Reeves directing the movies. If true, this means that Reeves leaving would always be tied to Pattinson's departure. This also lines up with recent reports that the constant delays of The Batman: Part II allowed Pattinson to get out of his contract for the third movie. There were also rumors that Amazon MGM wasn't going to allow Pattinson to make Batman and James Bond movies at the same time, so this was coming no matter what.

articles.title: GTA 6 PS5 Sales Near 39 Million & Obliterate an All-Time PlayStation Record
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Rockstar Games Grand Theft Auto 6 seemed destined to break records, and now it's becoming more clear exactly what those records are. PlayStation has just spoken about how well GTA 6 has done on PS5 in the few days since launch, revealing certain stats and milestones that demonstrate a record-shattering weekend for the console manufacturer. As stated […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Grand Theft Auto 6 seemed destined to break records, and now it's becoming more clear exactly what those records are . PlayStation has just spoken about how well GTA 6 has done on PS5 in the few days since launch, revealing certain stats and milestones that demonstrate a record-shattering weekend for the console manufacturer.

As stated on the PlayStation Blog , GTA 6 has reached 39 million players on PS5. Strangely, it doesn't explicitly spell out how many units were sold — it's possible account sharing helped boost the numbers here — but the real number likely isn't too far off from 39 million. For context, Marvel's Spider-Man 2 is considered a smash hit and, as of August, has sold 18 million units in the three or so years since launch. Rockstar Games previously shared GTA 6 had sold 32.5 million copies across both PS5 and Xbox Series X|S on it first day alone, showing how much word of mouth and overwhelmingly positive buzz has equaled a few million more sales.

These staggering numbers, according to PlayStation, have made GTA 6 's launch the biggest launch on PlayStation hardware across the five home consoles and two handhelds. As of November 22nd, it also had the highest number of concurrent players for game on PlayStation, which includes free-to-play games like Fortnite and other heavy hitters like Call of Duty. Cumulatively, player spent around 683 million hours in Leonida on PlayStation from launch to November 22nd, and clocked an average of 17.4 hours in the game.

Many of these players were new to the PS5, as well. PlayStation noted the well-reviewed open-world game launch saw the biggest number of new consoles connecting online since the PS5's launch in November 2020 "outside of end-of-year" holidays, meaning this wasn't the largest weekend ever for new PS5s, but it was among them.

Also, GTA 6 was the first game played on 70% of these brand-new PS5s. This is quite impressive, too, since the console comes pre-loaded with Astro's Playroom and the game itself is around 210 GB , showing the determination and patience of those who wanted to play GTA 6 before anything else. Astro's Playroom also shot up in list of the most-played PS5 titles, which illustrated how at least some dabbled in their new free PS5 game even if it wasn't their first choice.

Other analysts have chimed in with various reports and projections speaking to GTA 6 's success, too. According to reliable research firm Circana, PS5 console sales shot up 2.4 times in the week ending in November 7th compared to the same week in 2025. Xbox Series X|S hardware sales went up 2.3 times during that same window, as well. Gaming market data firm Alinea Analytics also estimated the game had sold 44.9 million units, with 33.7 million on PS5 and 11.2 million on Xbox Series X|S. These are just estimates and PlayStation's use of "unique players" instead of hard units sold mean there probably won't be exact sales data until Rockstar inevitably reveals another milestone.

Xbox, on the other hand, hasn't come out with any other sort of official stats. Given the install base and PlayStation's heavy marketing push , its batch of stats are likely going to be vastly inferior by comparison, even if they set some records for the green-tinted console maker. Xbox has also had to talk around GTA 6 in some instances, likely due to PlayStation's aforementioned marketing deal with Rockstar. For example, Xbox was giving out fake doctor's notes so players could take a few days off for the "BIG week" in gaming, gesturing at GTA 6 without saying it. The company also held a sweepstakes for an Xbox inside of an alligator, another reference to the gator-infested lands of Leonida.

Is this more or less what you expected from Grand Theft Auto 6 ? Let us know in the comments.

The series beat out Steven Knight’s Hulu boxing drama A Thousand Blows ; Prime Video's Argentine political drama Menem ; and underdog sports drama Real Kashmir Football Club from Indian pay-TV group Sony LIV.

articles.title: Why I Have Mixed Feelings On How 90 Day: Hunt For Love Addressed Razvan’s Exit
articles.summary: It's a difficult thing to address.
articles.content:
Warning! The following contains spoilers for the 90 Day: Hunt For Love episode "The Boy Who Left His Mark." Stream the episode with an HBO Max subscription , and read at your own risk!

For those unaware, Razvan was removed from 90 Day: Hunt For Love after he allegedly used a racial slur to refer to Jamal Menzies during their argument. Rather than show the incident, the 90 Day Fiancé show decided instead to flash the following text onscreen before moving on to the next day:

The scene then switched to Iris meeting up with the other 90 Day: Hunt For Love singles and explaining that he left. There was no discussion about what happened, and it was more to state that Iris was "back on the market" with her match gone. Had someone watching only learned of the incident from the 2026 TV schedule , they wouldn't have known what happened.

I don't know all the context that went into this decision, but I can already see some problems with it. To start, I don't think avoiding what happened with Razvan is going to dissuade viewers out of the loop from looking up what happened. He was a prominent part of 90 Day: Hunt For Love up to this point, and I think his absence will be felt.

articles.title: David Zaslav Recalls "Awkward Moment" Before Skydance Merger Close, Hails Ex-WBD Global Chief Gerhard Zeiler For Keeping Staff "Motivated"

articles.content:
In one of his first public appearances since the close of the $110 billion Skydance merger, ex- Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav on Monday recalled a key sequence during the deal's regulatory review.

"We were in this awkward moment," Zaslav said Monday at the International Emmys in New York. "We had a hearing, we needed to keep the entire company motivated."

Gerhard Zeiler , WBD's former international chief, decided to visit all of the company's global offices, Zaslav remembered. "There was a lot of trepidation, and people were concerned about their own jobs, and where would they be, and how would they, how would this affect their families. When it comes down to it, we're all just people," he said in presenting Zeiler with the International Emmys Directorate Award. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories News Skydance Buyouts Impact CBS Stations; Local Chicago Anchor Among Those Departing News SkyShowtime Staff Complained About Workplace Culture & Handling Of "Racist Conduct" Before Comcast/Skydance Shuttered Streamer

After the streaming giant initially secured a deal for Warner's streaming and studio assets, Paramount then prevailed in a proposal accepted last February by the WBD board. "In those first few weeks [after Paramount had emerged as the proposed acquirer], I got very caught up in the transaction. I would call Gerhardt, and each time I called him, I would ask him, 'Where are you?' And you could tell me a different city," Zaslav said, looking across the stage at Zeiler. "Finally, after about a month, and 15 different places that he had visited, I said, 'How many countries are you gonna go to? What are you doing?' And he said, 'You know, this is a really tough time for the employees. It's difficult, and I want to go, and I want to meet with everyone, I'm going face to face. I want about lunch. I want to go to dinner.'" Zaslav noted Zeiler's "working-class" origins and his rise to lead "the largest international media company in the world, now even larger, with this great merger, with Paramount." On the week of the merger's completion, Zeiler said confirmed he was stepping away after a lengthy run at the company, opting to enter the political arena in his native Austria.

The former CEO also said Zeiler "fought inside our company for local content," especially on flagship streamer HBO Max, which had a major reboot and global relaunch during the Zaslav-Zeiler years. "The feeling was, we can just push out the great content that we have at Warner Brothers, the great HBO content, on all of our channels. You can rely on a library. But he fought hard, and he never stopped, and it was one of the great strategic advantages for us. And we had local content in every one of these markets, and local sports, and local news. And it made us so much more relevant."

Zeiler's acceptance speech was straightforward and a fair bit shorter than Zaslav's introduction.

He called his run at WBD and its predecessors (and RTL before that) "a journey to which I never stopped learning. Not one single day. And you get to know this nuances, the differences, specialties of the individual cultures all around the world. That was the biggest gig I got in my professional life."

articles.title: Antoine Fuqua Accused of Pointing Handgun, Using Antisemitic Slur in Assault Lawsuit
articles.summary: A spokesperson for the director denied the allegations and said, "It's not true."
articles.content:
Director Antoine Fuqua has been sued for assault and battery by a bar manager, who alleges the director struck him with a handgun and used an antisemitic slur.

In a lawsuit filed on Friday in California state court, the bar manager, William Rosenthal, details an altercation in February in which Fuqua and his group were denied entry to a Los Angeles bar because they were overly intoxicated. He claims the director "directed a racial and antisemitic slur" at him before the filmmaker and his son "pointed their handguns" in his direction. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Business Selena Gomez's Wondermind Fraud Lawsuit Has Been Dismissed With Prejudice TV Chris Pratt Seeks Violent Redemption in 'The Terminal List' Season 2 First-Look Images

Rosenthal brings claims for assault, battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress. He seeks at least $50,000.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the director denied the allegations. "It's not true," the representative said.

The lawsuit says Fuqua and four others, including his daughter and son, visited Good Times at Davey Wayne's in Los Angeles on Feb. 14. After the group was refused entry by Rosenthal, he was spat on by a member of the group and threatened by Fuqua's daughter, according to the complaint. They left the establishment, the lawsuit says.

Roughly an hour later, Fuqua returned and confronted Rosenthal about pepper spraying his daughter. Rosenthal denied the accusation and was hit in the face with a handgun by the director, who later used an antisemitic slur and threatened to kill the bar manager. From there, the altercation escalated, with Fuqua's son also pulling out a handgun and striking Rosenthal, the lawsuit says.

Rosenthal says he sustained a head injury, nose fracture and lacerations from the alleged assault and now has post-traumatic stress disorder and severe emotional stress. His lawyers say the injuries will result in "some permanent disability."

articles.title: Adam Driver Reveals The Major Personal Sacrifice He Was Going to Make to Get The Hunt for Ben Solo Made
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Lucasfilm Adam Driver said he was developing The Hunt for Ben Solo for free to try to get Disney to make the movie. Driver had wanted to return to the Star Wars franchise as Ben Solo more than anything for a long time. He also had fans behind him as he tried to get the movie […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Adam Driver said he was developing The Hunt for Ben Solo for free to try to get Disney to make the movie. Driver had wanted to return to the Star Wars franchise as Ben Solo more than anything for a long time. He also had fans behind him as he tried to get the movie made. While the Star Wars sequels were polarizing with many fans, once they were finished, fans wanted to see more of Driver as Ben Solo, who was known as Kylo Ren throughout the three movies. However, while the movie was in development, Disney decided not to follow through with it for a ridiculous reason. The studio said it didn't make sense for Kylo to return since he died in the movies, even though Palpatine returned to the sequels after dying in the original trilogy.

Adam Driver appeared on Sam Fragoso’s Talk Easy podcast and talked about the movie, and he admitted to what both he and Steven Soderbergh did to try to get the movie made. "Soderbergh did that for nothing because we were given a lot of confidence," Driver said. "We worked on it, and no one was paying us to work on it. The only reason why we’re working on it is because we f—ing loved the idea, how we wanted to do it. And I loved that character, and that was it."

Adam Driver and Steven Soderbergh Worked for Free on The Hunt for Ben Solo Image Courtesy of Lucasfilm Adam Driver also said in the interview that he, Steven Soderbergh, and Kathleen Kennedy were trying to make The Hunt for Ben Solo on a smaller budget to ensure that it got made. He said the financial side came later because they wanted to ensure it was cheap enough to allow him and Soderbergh to do what they wanted to do with the movie. However, what is most shocking is that Disney executives said they didn't understand how Ben Solo could return after dying in Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker . That didn't make any sense because Palpatine's return from the dead was explained in the sequels as "Somehow, Palpatine returned.

Driver had said all along that he was open to returning as Ben Solo if the story and director were great. That is when Soderbergh showed up, and he began to work with Jules Asner on creating a story outline. Kennedy was receptive to the idea, and then they brought in Scott Z. Burns to write the screenplay. Driver had everything he wanted. He had Soderbergh as a great director and a script that he said was one of the "coolest" ones that he has ever been a part of. That was when Bob Iger and Alan Bergman rejected the project after the team pitched it to them.

Driver has been very vocal about the rejection this year, including saying that it was "criminal" not to make the movie, especially with Soderbergh as the director. Now, with Driver saying that he and Soderbergh were willing to work on the movie for free, it speaks volumes about how much the two of them wanted to see this story make it to the big screen. Whatever happens, The Hunt for Ben Solo might be one of the biggest missed opportunities in the Star Wars universe.

articles.title: From Beauty to Tech, Deep Black Friday Deals Land on the New Brand+ Marketplace via AliExpress
articles.summary: Launched late last year, the Brand+ channel is a dedicated shopping destination for products from trusted brands.
articles.content:
In November 2025, online retailer AliExpress made a big move towards credibility: the introduction of Brand+, a dedicated shopping destination for trusted products from both household names and emerging brands. Now, Brand+ is hosting its second-ever Black Friday Sale, with deep price drops on its already-discounted selection.

Since debuting just over a year ago, the Brand+ inventory has consistently grown in scope, spanning fan-favorite labels across audio, toys, tech and fashion. articles.title: The X-Men Got Iceman's Coming-Out Story Wrong, but the MCU Has a Chance to Get It Right
articles.summary: The X-Men are coming back to the big screen as part of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, something that fans have been asking for since the MCU became massive in the '10s. I'm one of those Marvel fans who thinks that Marvel Studios has never been as good as adapting the Marvel Universe as others do […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The X-Men are coming back to the big screen as part of the Marvel Cinematic Universe , something that fans have been asking for since the MCU became massive in the '10s. I'm one of those Marvel fans who thinks that Marvel Studios has never been as good as adapting the Marvel Universe as others do (and I've been of this opinion since the early to mid '10s; if you want to hunt down my old Facebook posts, you'll see that), but even I can admit that they will do a better job of adapting things than Fox ever did. Everyone enjoyed the FoX-Men movies, but they weren't great adaptations as far as comic accuracy goes. There are plenty of places where I think Marvel Studios will do a great job adapting, but there are also things I don't want them to adapt very faithfully, like Iceman 's coming out as gay.

The story of Iceman's homosexuality is one of the most contentious in comics for a variety of reasons. To begin with, there's this idea that you can never change the sexuality of established characters, that they can only be gay or straight or bi or ace or whatever the whole time. No one is allowed to come out of the closet for some fans, something that is honestly pretty common in the real world. These fans started an uproar over the very concept of gay Iceman. For the purposes of this article, we're only going to bring up those people mockingly, because their reasoning is never sound and I say that as someone who has been reading Iceman since he was with Opal Tanaka. However, there are fans who hate it for the right reasons – it's one of the worst coming out moments ever. Looking at the history of the character, it honestly makes all the sense in the world that he was gay, but the problem, one that the MCU can solve easily , is the coming out moment itself.

So, to begin with, let's get this out of the way – Bobby Drake wasn't created to be gay, but then again, none of those original superheroes were. It was a different time in American pop culture and you wouldn't get a gay character in what was essentially children's media back in the day. For his early years, Iceman was a straight character. However, he was also the class clown, the one who never grew up. His romantic relationships, like the aforementioned Opal Tanaka, were fine but never really felt right. Honestly, if you know people who came out later in life, Bobby shares a lot of similarities with them.

Now, back then, all of this was inadvertent, but starting in the '90s, creators like Fabian Nicieza started to hint that maybe Bobby wasn't as plumb as an arrow, if you catch my drift. There's one now-famous scene of him out shopping with Jean Grey that definitely feels like the precursor to him coming out. However, it was the '90s, "Onslaught" was about to happen, and that moment was forgotten. Bobby joined the ranks of Omega-level X-Men in the '90s, so you can see how creators were trying to change him. They even did a story that involved his father sticking up for him as a mutant after years as a bigot. It all felt like it was going in a certain direction, but it didn't.

It wouldn't be until the 2012 Bendis run on X-Men that all of this would start to get paid off and it's where we get to the real problem with the reveal. Bendis played Bobby as the young girl-crazy member of the team, but it started to feel hollow as it went on, leading to Jean Grey telling him that she had been reading his mind and it was time to be honest with himself about his sexuality. It was, honestly, the worst way you could do a character coming out. Jean basically forced him to take a look at his life that he wasn't ready for. It's everything you're not supposed to do with someone who hasn't come out of the closet.

So, while we got the somewhat expected braindead clamoring of the bigots, we also got people who honestly felt like it was a terrible coming out moment that damaged two characters. Bendis was trying to tell a story with Jean at the time about her becoming too powerful, too fast and using her greater powers irresponsibility, I think as a way to telegraph that this sort of behavior was always a part of Jean to show why "The Dark Phoenix Saga" happened. It made sense to an extent, since telepathy is an easy to abuse power, but it also didn't really fit the Jean Grey we knew. It damaged Iceman because it took away all of his agency in a moment that should have been about him.

Much like Alan Scott being made gay in 2011, being gay fit Iceman's history perfectly. It made it all make sense, but the way he was outed took away any momentum the moment had because it became about Jean's actions rather than the gay person finally getting to be honest with themselves. It's one of those moments that was written to be positive but was done in a such a way that ended up making it exactly the opposite. In the years since, Iceman barely had an identity as a gay man because of it; sure, we get him dating and hooking up, which is a step in the right direction (straight people often write queer couples in traditional relationships to make them "safer" for people used to heteronormativity) but it mostly feels like going through the motions.

The MCU can fix all of this. Iceman is a founding X-Men who played a big role in the FoX-Men movies, so he's basically a lock for the MCU. Marvel Studios will have him come out of the closet at some point or introduce him as gay, but I think the latter is the wrong way to go with the character. It would be better to give him a coming out of the closet journey. It would give him a great story, putting some spotlight on him, and it could be used to show what coming out is for an audience that doesn't really get stories like this.

Marvel Studios has already established Jean as something of a mad dog telepath; I think that Spider-Man: Brand New Day Jean is the kind of person who would out someone thinking that she was helping them. However, it's also a terrible look for the character, so I hope they don't go this way. Instead, I think a more organic coming process, one that allowed the character and the audience to see what it's like together, is the way to go. It would be a better story and it would be about the actual gay person, Iceman, rather than the straight girl.

What do you think about Iceman's coming out moment? Do you think that Marvel Studios should do it differently? How? Sound off in the comment section below.

articles.title: Vin Diesel's Panned 24-Year-Old Attempt to Be James Bond Is About to Get Harder to Watch in December
articles.summary: Courtesy of Columbia Pictures Vin Diesel may be best know for his appearances in The Fast and Furious franchise, but he has spent many years attempting to kickstart other franchises that could have been just as big as his high-octane, star-studded street-racing-turned-space-travelling saga. One such movie was released in 2002, when Diesel attempted to muscle into the action spy […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Vin Diesel may be best know for his appearances in The Fast and Furious franchise , but he has spent many years attempting to kickstart other franchises that could have been just as big as his high-octane, star-studded street-racing-turned-space-travelling saga. One such movie was released in 2002, when Diesel attempted to muscle into the action spy genre and become a bigger, louder James Bond in his role as extreme-sports daredevil Xander Cage in xXx . While the movie did generate a couple of sequels - although Diesel only returned for one of them, the movie was not the great success it could have been and has often been called one of the actor's most incoherent and wildly over-the-top movies - which is quite a feat when glancing back through his catalog of acting roles. Now, those who do have a soft spot for Diesel's xXx have only a limited time left to watch it before it leaves Netflix on December 1.

In 2002, Diesel was coming off the success of The Fast and the Furious a year earlier, and a reteaming with that movie's director Rob Cohen seemed like the best route to another hit for the actor. The film follows Diesel's Xander Cage as he is recruited by Samuel L. Jackson's NSA handler Augustus Gibbons to infiltrate a dangerous group of Russian terrorists. Costarring Asia Argento and Marton Csokas, the film was billed as James Bond meets punk rock - even knowingly having a tuxedo-wearing spy killed off in its opening sequence to send a message - but after landing itself a 48% Rotten Tomatoes score, it became clear that the film was a very divisive affair. Even with renowned critic Roger Ebert surprisingly fighting its corner with a three and a half stars score and comment that "in its own punk way, xXx is as good as a good Bond movie," the film couldn't quite manage to please the majority.

Despite coming with a title that could cause many problems for search engine results, xXx is a film that probably deserved more attention and love than it received. Audiences were a little more onboard with the chaotic and frantic action flick, giving it a 58% Popcornmeter rating, with many recent reviews pointing out that while the movie may be "big and dumb," it is not the worst way to pass a couple of hours. Some call it "a pretty decent action movie if you don't mind the action being completely unbelievable," others call it "the worst movie I've ever seen." That kind of vastly differing opinion did not hurt the movie's box office performance as it turned a reasonable $80 million budget into a $277 million gross. That of course led to a sequel, xXx: State of the Union , in 2005, but this time it was Ice Cube in the driving seat with Diesel passing on a return.

In 2017, 15 years after his previous appearance, Diesel unexpectedly did return to the franchise in the blatantly titled, xXx: The Return of Xander Cage. Reviews of the movie were even more brutal than the original, but once again, coming in the wake of several huge Fast & Furious movies , Diesel's xXx comeback led to a $346 million worldwide haul, and although a fourth movie has been discussed , it has yet to really get any traction. While Diesel may have starred in other more popular movies, those looking to have a blast without thinking too hard about it could do worse than to track down xXx before it leaves Netflix on December 1.

Does xXx deserve more love? Would you come back for a second viewing if you have already seen it? Let us know in the comments.

Fincher envisioned a group of prisoners who had been written off by society realizing that the one good thing they could do with their lives was make sure the Xenomorph died with them.

Much of that pitch actually made it into Alien 3 . What's particularly telling about Fincher's approach to the movie, though, is how much thought he'd given to the evolution of the franchise under Ridley Scott and James Cameron. Fincher saw a progression in what Ellen Ripley (Sigourney Weaver) was willing to risk her life for between the first two movies. He wanted to put Ripley in the company of men whose lives were considered expendable and explore what they would be willing to give their lives for. Speaking with Josh Horowitz on the Happy Sad Confused podcast , Fincher explained how he arrived at the pitch that sold Weaver and the producers on him directing the movie.

David Fincher Wanted Alien 3 to Be a Movie About Redemption Fincher considers the original Alien one of the 10 greatest movies ever made. He loves that Scott gets the audience to disagree with Ripley's decision not to let Kane, played by John Hurt, back aboard the Nostromo. The crew wants to save Kane's life, even though Ripley is the only person adhering to the protocol to keep everyone alive. As Fincher points out, 15 minutes later, we're all thinking, "We should have listened to the tall girl." Despite the considerable differences between Scott and Cameron's movies, Fincher sees a throughline in their treatment of Ripley. "The first movie is go back for the cat, and the second movie is go back for the child," explained Fincher. Ripley goes from risking her life for Jonesy in Alien to essentially becoming a mother again in Aliens .

Fincher's pitch for Alien 3 took into consideration how little regard the people in power in the Alien universe have for human life. If Weyland-Yutani was willing to sacrifice the crew of the Nostromo to get its hands on a Xenomorph, what chance did the inhabitants of a prison colony have? "We are all going to die tonight," Fincher said of the realization he wanted the prisoners to come to. "The only face-saving that we can do here is to take that thing with us."

Perhaps the best argument for Fincher's original pitch is the performance Charles S. Dutton gives in Alien 3 . Dillon has already devoted much of his life to seeking redemption through religion. Ripley's arrival on Fiorina 161 affords him and the other prisoners an opportunity to find it. The 2003 Assembly Cut of Alien 3 benefits considerably from the additional time we get to spend with these men before Ripley asks them to help her kill the creature. What makes Fincher's pitch such a good follow-up to the first two movies is that Ripley is now asking other people to make the kind of decision she's made twice before. Nobody would blame these men for wanting to get as far away from the creature as possible. They may well be the last people in the universe who owe humanity anything. And yet, they're the ones tasked with saving it.

Fincher may not like his own movie, but it has gained a considerable following from devoted fans like Christopher Nolan. Perhaps on your next watch, the film can hit a little different knowing what Fincher's ambitions were. Do you love Alien 3 ? Let us know what you think in the comments below.

articles.title: James Gunn's DC Exit Has People Asking About Keanu Reeves And Constantine Again (& I Don’t Hate It)
articles.summary: Does this mean Constantine could be coming back soon?
articles.content:
With James Gunn and Peter Safran’s exiting DC , it's unknown if the DCU will continue or if we can expect yet another reboot. However, with one chapter closing for the studio, the start of a new might mean some long-gestating projects could get a second chance. Amid the corporate change, people have been asking about Keanu Reeves ' long-discussed Constantine sequel again, and honestly, I don’t hate the possibility of seeing the 2005 movie finally get a follow-up.

This is sure to be music to some fans' ears amid the major corporate shift. Jeremy Latcham, a Marvel Studios alum who worked with Gunn on Guardians of the Galaxy , is stepping into the role of DC Studios CEO. As a result, Gunn’s DC universe might be over , and Lawrence -- who's sympathetic to the exiting CEOs -- seems to be confident that this could open the door for a Constantine sequel.

2005's Constantine has earned quite the cult following. Believe it or not, Reeves wasn’t fans' first pick for the role, and that's because of how much of a departure from the comics his take on John is. The character has lived on in the live-action space since then, with Matt Ryan taking on the trench coat in 2014 for a short-lived NBC show. Ryan continued to portray Constantine in The CW’s Arrowverse and voiced the DC antihero in various animated works through 2024.

articles.title: DC Fans Can Save Years of Collecting With This Rare Swamp Thing Comic Lot
articles.summary: Sales for the original Swamp Thing may not have been strong, but the character has endured — incidentally turning those early issues into one of the most sought-after DC titles of its tumultuous Bronze Age. The Bronze Age was an era of growing pains for DC Comics, who were struggling to adapt to a changing […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Sales for the original Swamp Thing may not have been strong, but the character has endured — incidentally turning those early issues into one of the most sought-after DC titles of its tumultuous Bronze Age. The Bronze Age was an era of growing pains for DC Comics, who were struggling to adapt to a changing marketplace and increasingly stiff competition from Marvel. For readers, there was one clear benefit: the publisher understood themselves to be losing their grip on what was popular or appealing to its readers, and was willing to take risks. Editors let creatives push the comic book medium and the super-hero genre in new directions, and the result was some of the strangest, most exciting stories DC ever published. Jack Kirby's epic " Fourth World " saga emerged from this era, as did Denny O'Neil and Neal Adams' character-redefining Green Lantern / Green Arrow and Batman runs. However, few Bronze Age titles are as iconic or as sought-after as the original Len Wein and Bernie Wrightson issues of Swamp Thing .

Besides Kirby's aforementioned Fourth World titles ( The New Gods especially), few Bronze Age DC titles are as collectible as Swamp Thing 's first volume. Wrightson lent interiors and stunning covers to the first ten, while Wein scripted the first thirteen. This Heritage Auctions lot assembles the first twenty-one issues of Swamp Thing in a single lot, all in high-grade condition. The estimated value is listed by Heritage at around seven hundred and fifty dollars, but the real value of the lot is the time it saves the buyer. The lot includes all ten of the highly-sought after Bernie Wrightson-penciled issues, which usually necessitate years of patient collecting to assemble — as well as some hard questions about how much you're willing to pay and whether you're willing to compromise on condition.

Changing censorship standards in the early seventies allowed for horror comics — after being functionally banned for more than a decade — to make their return to newsstands. A generation of creators who had grown up on the controversial E.C. titles of the 1950s were entering the field, and were eager to lend their talents to the genre. Anthology titles like House of Mystery and House of Secrets were converted into horror books, and strong reader response supported an explosion of new horror titles like The Witching Hour, The Phantom Stranger , and The Demon . Swamp Thing was spun-off from a short story in House of Secrets #92, also by Wein and Wrightson. For the ongoing series, the duo retold the Southern gothic origin of the character, updating it for the modern era. While House of Secrets ' Alex Olsen became Swamp Thing because of a fire set by a romantic rival, Swamp Thing 's Alec Holland was killed for refusing to give over the secrets of his world-hunger ending bio-restorative formula to a shady criminal cabal. What didn't change was Wrightson's striking design for Swamp Thing, which resembles the artist's later interpretation of the Frankenstein Monster .

A more direct take on the Frankenstein Monster would come the following issue with the "Patchwork Man," a demented experiment by the mad Anton Arcane, who revives his brother Gregori from the dead after he's blown apart by a forgotten World War-era landmine. For Len Wein's initial thirteen issues especially, Swamp Thing existed in a dark, gothic world that — but for a team-up with Batman in Swamp Thing #7 — felt totally outside the DC Universe. It was a world of witches, eldritch horrors, and clockwork men, and every issue felt like it plunged Swamp Thing into a different nightmare out of Poe, Bierce, or Lovecraft. That was, however, Swamp Thing 's failing: Wein didn't know how to break Swamp Thing out of a "monster of the week" formula, and by the end of his thirteen-issue tenure, he felt the title was growing stale. The only real continuity thread was a Fugitive -esque subplot about Swamp Thing being pursued by federal agent Matt Cable, who mistakenly believes him responsible for Alec and Linda Holland's deaths. Subsequent writers David Michelinie and Gerry Conway had the same struggles, compounded by another mounting problem: waning reader interest.

The horror comic book explosion burned bright, but it did not burn for long. By the mid-seventies, titles like Tomb of Dracula , Werewolf by Night , and Swamp Thing were struggling to attract the strong readership of just a few years prior. Creators also found themselves burnt out, finding the storytelling potential of these character surprisingly limited. Swamp Thing 's final issues (by Gerry Conway, in collaboration with David Anthony Kraft for #24) attempted to revive the title by drastically changing its status quo: Alec Holland regains his humanity at the end of issue #23, and does not appear as Swamp Thing at all in the final issue. For the rest of the decade, Swamp Thing appeared only sporadically, serving as a supporting character to the Challengers of the Unknown (again written by Gerry Conway), as well as a guest star in team-up titles The Brave and the Bold and DC Comics Presents . The early issues were well-regarded by fans, but it wasn't enough to ensure a future — at least not until one of those fans bought the film rights.

Swamp Thing was a dormant character when entertainment lawyer, academic, and comic book geek Michael Uslan bought the film rights from DC. Uslan had been stymied by a years-long effort to get a darker, more grounded Batman film off the ground, and decided it would be easier to have creative control over a less well-known DC character. He chose Swamp Thing , feeling its stories and tone would be well-suited to adaptation. With Wes Craven in the director's chair, Uslan and business partner Benjamin Melniker set Swamp Thing for a 1982 release. To capitalize, DC decided to revive the Swamp Thing comic, launching Saga of the Swamp Thing at the same time as the film hit theaters. Saga of the Swamp Thing hit the same creative speed-bumps as its predecessor, and was due for cancellation by the time writer Martin Pasko left the series. Having little to lose by the decision, DC gave Saga of the Swamp Thing to a relative industry newcomer, British writer Alan Moore. Moore was told he could do as he liked with the title, given its precarious state.

The result was one of the most critically acclaimed comics ever published, turning Swamp Thing into one of DC's most popular characters among comic readers. Succeeded by penciller and co-plotter Rick Veitch, Moore's Swamp Thing brought complex, long-form storytelling to the character, taking it in strange directions in the process. Instead of a mutated Alec Holland, Swamp Thing was a plant that believed it was Alec Holland, the latest in a mystic line of "Guardians of the Green." This Swamp Thing was instrumental in the creation of DC's adult-oriented "Vertigo" imprint, as well as the gradual abandonment of the Comics Code Authority. It's perhaps best known for introducing John Constantine , routinely upheld alongside Swamp Thing as one of DC's best characters.

Although lauded for its experimentation and innovation, Moore and Veitch's Swamp Thing stayed rooted in the work of Wein and Wrightson, not only in using characters and ideas from the original run, but evoking its mood. Reprinted as The Roots of the Swamp Thing contemporaneously to Moore's ongoing, the first volume of Swamp Thing cemented itself as one of DC's most influential comics in the 1980s. It was at this time that those early issues took on their collectible status, which has only grown through the intervening decades as demand continues to outstrip supply. Both the Wein and the Moore runs of Swamp Thing have remained constantly in print since the rise of trade paperbacks and omnibuses, leaving new readers to discover their work every year. If they're lucky, it may be one such reader who wins the twenty-one issues of Swamp Thing on auction at Heritage, which planted the seed for the decades of Swamp Thing stories to follow.
